subject: Ceramics
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a practical paper. Two projects are set and the candidate executes one over five days at six hours a day, for 80 marks. The question paper arrives two weeks early, and the sketches and preparatory notes made in that time carry 20 marks, giving 100 marks in all.

practicals.title: Prospecting for clay and finding its water content
practicals.aim: To locate and sample a local clay deposit, carry out simple field tests, and find the water content of the sample.
apparatus: Notebook and phone camera or GPS
materials: Clay samples from a stream bank, valley bottom or old pottery site (for example Ikorodu, Okigwe, Kwali or Ushafa areas)
safety: Get permission from the landowner or community before you dig.
Do not dig under overhanging banks, which can collapse.
Wash your hands after handling the samples.
procedure: Look for signs of clay: cracked dry ground, sticky soil after rain, termite mounds, and riverbanks.
Remove the topsoil and humus. Dig down to the clay layer and record its depth, colour and thickness.

Field tests: rub a pinch between your fingers (smooth means clay, gritty means sand). Roll a coil 1 cm thick and bend it round a finger to test plasticity. Bite gently between your front teeth to feel for grit.
Bag and label each sample with the site, depth and date.
In school, weigh 250 g of the plastic clay, dry it to constant mass, and weigh it again.
practicals.expectedObservations: Good plastic clay feels smooth and sticky and bends without cracking. Sandy clays crack and feel gritty. Primary clays (kaolin) are white and less plastic. Secondary clays (ball clays, earthenware clays) are often grey, red or brown and more plastic.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Water content (dry basis) = (wet mass - dry mass) / dry mass x 100. Worked example: wet mass 250 g, dry mass 200 g, so water = 50 g and water content = 50 / 200 x 100 = 25%. On a wet basis it is 50 / 250 x 100 = 20%.
precautions: Remove all organic topsoil from the sample.
Dry the clay to constant mass.
Label the samples immediately.
sourcesOfError: The sample dries out between digging and weighing.
Mixing different layers in one sample.
commonMistakes: Not stating whether water content is on a wet or dry basis.
Collecting topsoil instead of clay.
examTips: Distinguish primary (residual) clay from secondary (sedimentary) clay by how it formed and its properties.
List the prospecting steps in order: locating, testing, sampling, recording.

checkQuestions.q: A clay weighs 300 g wet and 240 g dry. Its water content on a dry basis is
Kaolin is an example of
checkQuestions.explanation: Kaolin stays where it formed, so it is a primary (residual) clay.

checkQuestions.q: A coil that cracks badly when bent shows clay with
checkQuestions.explanation: Cracking on bending shows poor plasticity.

practicals.title: Drying and firing shrinkage test
practicals.aim: To find the drying, firing and total shrinkage of a clay body, and use the result to size a ware.
apparatus: Rolling pin and guide sticks (1 cm)
Kiln (or a well-managed open firing for a demonstration)
safety: Kiln work is supervised. Wear heat-resistant gloves and never open a hot kiln.
procedure: Roll a slab 1 cm thick and cut three test bars about 12 cm x 3 cm.
On each bar, scratch a straight line exactly 10.0 cm long between two fine marks. Label each bar.
Dry the bars slowly, turning them so they do not warp, then measure the line (dry length).
Bisque fire the bars (about 900 to 1000 degrees C) and measure the line again (fired length).
Calculate drying, firing and total shrinkage. Average the three bars.
practicals.expectedObservations: The line gets shorter after drying and shorter again after firing. Fine, plastic clays shrink more than sandy or grogged clays.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: plastic 10.0 cm, dry 9.4 cm, fired 8.9 cm. Drying shrinkage = (10.0 - 9.4) / 10.0 x 100 = 6%. Total shrinkage = (10.0 - 8.9) / 10.0 x 100 = 11%. Firing shrinkage (on the dry length) = (9.4 - 8.9) / 9.4 x 100 = 5.32%. To get a fired pot 20 cm high, make it 20 / (1 - 0.11) = 22.47 cm high when wet.
precautions: Make the marks fine and exact.
Dry the bars slowly and evenly to prevent warping.
Use the mean of several bars.
sourcesOfError: Reading the rule to too few decimal places.
commonMistakes: Calculating firing shrinkage on the plastic length instead of the dry length.
Adding the shrinkage to the finished size instead of dividing by (1 - shrinkage).
examTips: Show the formula, the substitution and the answer with % for each shrinkage.
Relate high shrinkage to defects (cracking, warping) and its cure (adding grog or sand).

checkQuestions.q: A 10 cm line measures 8.8 cm after firing. The total shrinkage is
A clay shrinks 10% in total. To get a 18 cm fired bowl, the wet size should be
Adding grog to a clay body mainly
checkQuestions.explanation: Grog opens the body and reduces shrinkage.

checkQuestions.q: Drying shrinkage is caused by
options: Loss of water from between the clay particles
checkQuestions.explanation: As water leaves, the particles move closer together.

practicals.title: Preparing clay: slaking, sieving, blending and wedging
practicals.aim: To prepare a smooth, plastic and air-free clay body from raw local clay.
apparatus: Plaster bats or a drying trough
safety: Dry clay dust contains silica. Damp-mop instead of sweeping and wear a dust mask when crushing dry clay.
Lift heavy buckets with a straight back.
procedure: Break the dry clay into small lumps and soak (slake) it in water for 24 hours.
Stir it into a slip and pour it through the sieve to remove stones, roots and sand.
Let the slip settle, pour off the clear water, and dry the slip on plaster bats until it is plastic.
Blend in other clays or grog by weight, if needed.
Wedge on the table using ram's head or spiral wedging, or cut-and-slam, until the cut faces show no air holes or streaks.
Store the clay wrapped in polythene so that it stays moist.
practicals.expectedObservations: Sieved, wedged clay is smooth and evenly coloured, and its cut faces show no air bubbles. Poorly wedged clay shows pockets and streaks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Blend 3 parts of a plastic local clay with 1 part kaolin to make 8 kg: plastic clay = 3/4 x 8 = 6 kg, kaolin = 1/4 x 8 = 2 kg. Adding grog at 10% of 6 kg of clay gives 0.6 kg.
precautions: Sieve thoroughly.
Do not let the clay dry too hard on the bats.
Wedge until there is no air.
commonMistakes: Folding air in by wedging carelessly.
Skipping the sieving, which leaves stones that cause blow-outs in the kiln.
examTips: Explain why air is removed: trapped air expands in the kiln and can burst the ware.
Name the equipment used in industry: blunger, filter press, pug mill.

checkQuestions.q: The main reason for wedging clay is to
options: Remove air and make it uniform
checkQuestions.explanation: Wedging removes air and evens the consistency.

checkQuestions.q: A 2:3 blend of clay A to clay B for 10 kg needs clay A of
The machine that de-airs and extrudes clay in industry is the
checkQuestions.explanation: A de-airing pug mill mixes and de-airs clay.

practicals.title: Hand building: a pinch pot and a coil-built vase
practicals.topic: Hand building, wheel work and casting
practicals.aim: To form a pinch pot and a coil vase of planned size with walls of even thickness.
apparatus: Serrated kidney or old hacksaw blade
safety: Keep the work area damp-clean to control dust.
Wash your hands.
procedure: Pinch pot: roll a ball, press your thumb into the centre, and pinch while turning so the wall is about 6 to 8 mm thick.
Coil vase: cut a base 12 cm in diameter from a slab 1 cm thick and score its edge.
Roll even coils about 1.5 cm thick. Score and slip, lay each coil on the one below, and blend the inside joints with your finger or a tool.
Check the profile against the card template. Place coils outward to widen the form and inward to narrow it.
Blend or texture the outside, scraping with a serrated kidney.
Cover with polythene between sessions. Finish the rim and sponge it smooth.
practicals.expectedObservations: Scored and slipped joints hold firm. Unscored joints crack on drying. The walls rise evenly if the coils are of the same thickness.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: One coil ring round a 12 cm base needs a length of pi x 12 = 37.70 cm. Each coil flattens to about 1.2 cm of wall height, so a 15 cm wall needs 15 / 1.2 = 12.5, or 13 coils. With 11% total shrinkage, a 15 cm wet height fires to 15 x 0.89 = 13.35 cm.
precautions: Score and slip every join.
Keep the wall thickness even.
Do not let the lower coils dry out before adding more.
sourcesOfError: Lower coils slumping when they are too wet.
commonMistakes: Building too fast, so the form collapses.
Not blending the inside joints.
examTips: Show the forming method, the templates and the measurements in your preparatory sketches.
Even walls, good form and a neat finish earn the technique marks.

checkQuestions.q: The coil length for one ring round a 10 cm diameter base is about
Joints in hand building are prepared by
checkQuestions.explanation: Scoring and slipping make a strong bond.

checkQuestions.q: Coils placed towards the outside of the wall make the form
checkQuestions.explanation: Placing coils outward widens the profile.

practicals.title: Slab building a cylinder and a box
practicals.topic: Hand building, wheel work and casting
practicals.aim: To roll even slabs and construct a cylindrical pen holder and a lidded box.
apparatus: Rolling pin and guide sticks (8 mm)
safety: Take care with knives.
Clean up clay dust damp.
procedure: Roll the clay on canvas between 8 mm guide sticks, turning the slab often.
Let the slabs stiffen to leather-hard for the box. Use them softer for the cylinder.
Cylinder: wrap newspaper around the 10 cm former, then wrap the slab around it. Bevel and overlap the join, score, slip and blend.
Box: cut the base and four walls from templates. Score and slip, join, and reinforce the inside corners with a thin coil.
Cut a lid with a flange, and test the fit.
Dry slowly under polythene.
practicals.expectedObservations: Leather-hard slabs stand upright and give crisp edges. Soft slabs sag. Wrapping the former in newspaper stops the clay sticking and allows for shrinkage.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Slab length for a cylinder 10 cm in diameter = pi x 10 = 31.42 cm, plus a 1.5 cm overlap = 32.92 cm, so about 33 cm. For a box with 10 cm sides and 0.8 cm walls, two walls are cut 10 cm wide and the other two are cut 10 - 2 x 0.8 = 8.4 cm wide to fit between them.
precautions: Use guide sticks for even thickness.
Join at leather-hard.
Dry slowly and evenly.
commonMistakes: Joining a soft slab to a dry slab, which cracks on drying.
Forgetting to allow for the wall thickness at the corners.
examTips: Draw working drawings with dimensions and allowances.
Mention leather-hard as the correct stage for joining slabs.

checkQuestions.q: The slab length for a cylinder 8 cm in diameter (no overlap) is about
The best stage for joining slab walls is
checkQuestions.explanation: Leather-hard clay is firm but still joinable.

checkQuestions.q: Guide sticks are used to give
checkQuestions.explanation: The rolling pin rides on the sticks.

practicals.title: Throwing a cylinder and a bowl on the potter's wheel
practicals.topic: Hand building, wheel work and casting
practicals.aim: To centre, open, pull up and shape clay on the wheel, then trim (turn) the foot at leather-hard.
materials: Well-wedged clay balls of about 500 g
safety: Tie back hair and loose clothing on electric wheels.
Keep electrical leads dry.
Start and stop the wheel with nothing touching it.
procedure: Slam the ball onto the wheel head. With the wheel fast and your hands wet and braced, cone the clay up and down until it runs true (centred).
Open with your thumbs to leave a base about 1 cm thick. Widen the base.
Pull up the walls in three or four pulls with the wheel at medium speed, thinning the clay evenly from the bottom upward.
Shape it (cylinder or bowl), compress the rim, and remove the slurry with a rib.
Wire the pot off and dry it to leather-hard.
Re-centre it upside down and trim the foot ring.
practicals.expectedObservations: Well-centred clay does not wobble against steady hands. Off-centre clay gives uneven walls. Too much water weakens the clay and the wall collapses.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: With 12% total shrinkage, a mug that must be 9 cm in diameter when fired is thrown 9 / (1 - 0.12) = 10.23 cm wide. Base thickness check: a needle shows 2 cm of clay above the wheel head, so trim about 1 cm off to leave 1 cm.
precautions: Centre properly before opening.
Sponge out water from the base.
Use the wheel slower as the pot widens.
sourcesOfError: Air bubbles left in the clay.
commonMistakes: Opening too deep, which leaves no base.
Pulling too fast or too wet, so the wall collapses.
examTips: Explain the stages in order: wedging, centring, opening, pulling, shaping, trimming.
Name the parts of the wheel and their uses.

checkQuestions.q: The first step after placing clay on the wheel is
checkQuestions.explanation: The clay must run true first.

checkQuestions.q: With 10% shrinkage, a fired cup 9 cm wide is thrown
Foot rings are trimmed when the pot is
checkQuestions.explanation: Leather-hard clay cuts cleanly.

practicals.title: Making a plaster mould for slip casting and press moulding
practicals.topic: Hand building, wheel work and casting
practicals.aim: To make a plaster of Paris mould, prepare casting slip of the right density, and cast and press-mould wares.
apparatus: Cottle boards or a lino strip
materials: Soft soap or another release agent
Casting slip (clay, water and a deflocculant such as sodium silicate)
safety: Wear a dust mask when sieving plaster and clay.
Never put plaster down the sink.
Setting plaster gets warm. Do not set a hand or body part in it.
procedure: Seal the model with soft soap and set it up inside the cottle, leaving about 3 cm of space all round.
Sprinkle the weighed plaster into the measured water, let it soak for 2 minutes, then stir gently without whipping in air. Pour it at once.
Leave it to set, remove the cottle and model, trim the edges, and dry the mould thoroughly.
Check the slip density by weighing 500 ml.
Fill the mould with slip and top it up. After 10 to 20 minutes, pour out the excess and drain upside down.
Release the cast when it shrinks from the mould. Fettle the seams and sponge.
Press moulding: press an even slab into a dry plaster dish mould, trim the rim, and release when firm.
practicals.expectedObservations: The dry plaster absorbs water and builds a wall of clay; a longer time gives a thicker wall. Slip that is too thin gives soft, slow casts, and slip that is too thick traps air.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Slip density: 500 ml weighs 880 g, so its specific gravity is 880 / 500 = 1.76 (a typical target is about 1.75 to 1.80). Plaster at about 1.4 kg per litre of water: 1.4 kg of plaster takes up about 1.4 / 2.63 = 0.53 L, so each litre of water yields about 1.53 L of mix. To fill 6.0 L you need water 6.0 / 1.53 = 3.92 L and plaster 3.92 x 1.4 = 5.48 kg.
precautions: Add plaster to water, never water to plaster.
Dry the mould fully before casting.
Use a release agent on the model.
sourcesOfError: Measuring errors in plaster and water.
commonMistakes: Whipping air into the plaster.
Draining too early, which leaves thin walls.
examTips: Explain the role of the deflocculant: it keeps the slip fluid with less water.
Mention avoiding undercuts, or using two-piece moulds.

checkQuestions.q: 1000 ml of slip weighs 1,780 g. Its specific gravity is
In mixing plaster you should
checkQuestions.explanation: Plaster is sifted into the water.

checkQuestions.q: Wall thickness in slip casting depends mainly on
options: Time the slip stays in the mould
checkQuestions.explanation: The longer the slip stays, the thicker the wall.

practicals.title: Surface decoration: incising, stamping, sgraffito, slip trailing and sprigging
practicals.aim: To decorate leather-hard wares with a planned motif using several decorative techniques.
apparatus: Stamps (carved wood, bottle tops, seeds, or rolled roulettes)
materials: Coloured slips (white slip, and red slip with iron oxide)
safety: Handle the sharp tools carefully.
Wear a mask when mixing oxides into slip.
procedure: Divide the rim or surface into equal sections using a strip of paper.
Incise lines with the needle tool, and impress textures with stamps or roulettes.
Sgraffito: coat a section with contrasting slip, let it lose its shine, then scratch through to the clay body.
Slip trailing: squeeze lines and dots of slip onto the surface.
Sprigging: press clay into a small mould, score and slip the back, and attach it.
Let the work dry slowly. Record each technique on labelled test tiles.
practicals.expectedObservations: Decoration on leather-hard clay is crisp. On wet clay it smears and on dry clay it chips. Sgraffito shows a clear two-colour contrast.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A bowl rim 18 cm in diameter has a circumference of pi x 18 = 56.55 cm. Eight equal motifs need 56.55 / 8 = 7.07 cm each (or 360 / 8 = 45 degrees apart).
precautions: Decorate at the right moisture stage.
Score and slip every sprig.
Plan the divisions before you start cutting.
sourcesOfError: Slip that is too thick flakes off.
commonMistakes: Cutting too deep and weakening the wall.
Unattached sprigs falling off in the kiln.
examTips: Name each technique correctly and say at which stage it is done.
Relate motifs to local culture (uli, nsibidi, adinkra-type symbols).

checkQuestions.q: Scratching through a slip layer to show the body is
checkQuestions.explanation: Sgraffito means scratched.

checkQuestions.q: Twelve motifs round a circle are spaced at
checkQuestions.explanation: 360 / 12 = 30 degrees.

checkQuestions.q: Sprigs are attached by
checkQuestions.explanation: Score and slip the joint.

practicals.title: Drying and bisque firing with a firing schedule
practicals.aim: To dry wares safely, pack and bisque fire a kiln following a planned schedule, and compare it with open firing.
apparatus: Electric or fuel kiln with a pyrometer, or an open-firing pit
materials: Firewood, grass and straw for open firing
safety: Only fire under teacher supervision.
Never open a hot kiln.
Keep fuels and the open fire away from buildings.
Use gloves and goggles when looking into the spyhole.
procedure: Dry the ware slowly, covered at first, then in the open air until bone dry (it is no longer cold to touch on the cheek).
Pack the kiln: greenware may touch, but stack heavy pieces at the bottom and keep pieces off the elements.
Fire slowly to 600 degrees C at about 100 degrees C per hour, with the vents open for water smoking (up to about 200 degrees C) and the burn-off of carbon.
Fire more quickly from 600 to the bisque temperature of about 1000 degrees C.
Switch off and let the kiln cool naturally before unpacking.
For open firing, pre-heat the pots near the fire, cover them with fuel, burn, and let them cool in the ash.
Plot temperature against time.
practicals.expectedObservations: Properly dried and slowly heated wares come out sound and ring when tapped. Damp ware or fast early heating causes cracks or explosions. Open-fired wares are darker and often smoke-marked.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Schedule: 30 to 600 degrees C at 100 degrees C per hour takes (600 - 30) / 100 = 5.7 h. 600 to 1000 degrees C at 150 degrees C per hour takes 400 / 150 = 2.67 h. Total heating = 8.37 h, about 8 h 22 min. Quartz inversion at 573 degrees C is why heating and cooling are slow through that range.
precautions: Fire only bone-dry ware.
Heat slowly through the water-smoking stage and quartz inversion.
Leave vents open early in the firing.
commonMistakes: Firing damp ware, which explodes.
Opening the kiln too early, which causes dunting (cooling cracks).
examTips: Distinguish bisque (biscuit) firing from glost (glaze) firing.
Label a firing graph with temperature (degrees C) against time (h).

checkQuestions.q: Heating from 25 to 625 degrees C at 120 degrees C per hour takes
Quartz inversion takes place at about
checkQuestions.explanation: Quartz changes form at about 573 degrees C.

checkQuestions.q: The first firing of unglazed ware is called
checkQuestions.explanation: Bisque or biscuit firing.

checkQuestions.q: A pot exploding early in firing usually means it was
checkQuestions.explanation: Water turning to steam bursts the ware.

practicals.title: Preparing, applying and firing a glaze, and spotting defects
practicals.aim: To weigh out a glaze batch from a percentage recipe, apply it by dipping, pouring or spraying, glost fire it, and identify glaze defects.
safety: Wear a dust mask and gloves. Glaze materials are harmful if inhaled or swallowed, and silica dust damages the lungs.
Use only lead-free glazes for food ware.
Clean up with a damp cloth.
procedure: Calculate the batch from the percentage recipe and weigh each material.
Mix with water to the consistency of single cream and sieve it twice.
Wax the foot of each bisque ware, or wipe the base clean.
Glaze by dipping (count to 3), pouring for the insides, or spraying in a booth to an even thickness of about 1 mm.
Sponge glaze off the foot. Place the wares on the kiln shelf so that they do not touch each other.
Glost fire to the glaze's maturing temperature, then cool slowly.
Examine the results and identify any defects.
practicals.expectedObservations: A well-applied glaze fires smooth and glossy. Defects include crawling (glaze pulling back from dusty or greasy areas), pinholing, crazing (a mismatch in expansion), running (too thick or overfired), and a dull surface (underfired).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Recipe: frit 70%, kaolin 10%, silica 20%, plus 1% cobalt oxide. For a 2,000 g batch: frit 0.70 x 2000 = 1,400 g, kaolin 200 g, silica 400 g, cobalt oxide 0.01 x 2000 = 20 g.
precautions: Sieve the glaze to mix it evenly.
Keep the foot free of glaze.
Stir often during use, because glazes settle.
commonMistakes: Glazing the foot, which sticks the ware to the shelf.
Applying glaze too thickly, so it runs.
examTips: Link each defect to its cause and cure.
Show batch calculations as a table.

checkQuestions.q: Silica at 25% of a 1,600 g batch is
Glaze pulling back to leave bare patches is
checkQuestions.explanation: Crawling is often caused by dust or grease.

checkQuestions.q: Fine cracks in a fired glaze are called
checkQuestions.explanation: Crazing comes from the glaze contracting more than the body.

practicals.title: Colouring oxide test tiles (line blend)
practicals.aim: To find the colours given by different percentages of colouring oxides in a base glaze.
safety: Wear a mask and gloves, because oxides are toxic.
Label every container.
Wash your hands before eating.
procedure: Number the test tiles and record the oxide and the percentage on the back of each.
For each 100 g of base glaze, add the oxide at 2%, 4% and 6%.
Mix each with water, apply evenly to its tile, and leave one tile with base glaze only as the control.
Fire all the tiles together in the same glost firing.
Arrange the fired tiles in order and record the colours.
practicals.expectedObservations: In an oxidising firing, iron gives honey, amber or brown. Copper gives greens. Cobalt gives strong blues even at 0.5 to 1%. Manganese gives purple-brown. Colour deepens as the percentage rises.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For 100 g of base glaze: 2% = 2 g, 4% = 4 g, 6% = 6 g of iron oxide. For a 250 g batch at 4%: 0.04 x 250 = 10 g.
precautions: Apply the same thickness to every tile.
Fire all the tiles in the same firing.
Weigh carefully.
sourcesOfError: Small weighing errors at low percentages.
Position in the kiln changes the temperature.
commonMistakes: Not labelling tiles.
Leaving out a control tile.
examTips: Know the colour each oxide gives and the effect of the firing atmosphere.
Distinguish oxides, stains and underglazes.

checkQuestions.q: In an oxidising glaze, cobalt oxide gives
checkQuestions.explanation: Cobalt gives strong blue.

checkQuestions.q: Copper at 3% of 300 g of glaze is
Iron oxide in an oxidising glaze tends to give
checkQuestions.explanation: Iron gives honey, amber and browns.

practicals.title: Designing and making ceramic hand tools
practicals.topic: Design and construction of ceramic tools and equipment
practicals.aim: To design and make a set of modelling tools, a cutting wire, rolling guides and a loop tool from local materials.
materials: Hardwood strip (1 m x 2 cm x 0.5 cm)
safety: Cut away from your body and clamp the work in the vice.
Wear goggles when filing metal.
Smooth all edges so that they will not cut your hands.
procedure: Draw full-size working drawings of each tool with dimensions.
Mark out and saw the hardwood into 18 cm lengths.
Shape the ends (pointed, flat, rounded or serrated) with the knife and file, then sand them smooth and oil them.
Cutting wire: cut 60 cm of wire, tie a toggle to each end, and twist the ends secure.
Loop tool: bend a steel strip into a loop and bind it into a slotted wooden handle.
Rolling guides: cut two strips of equal thickness (for example 6 mm) and check them with callipers.
Test each tool on clay and improve it.
practicals.expectedObservations: Smooth, well-balanced tools leave clean marks. Rough wood drags and tears the clay.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A 1 m (100 cm) strip cut into 18 cm tools gives 100 / 18 = 5.56, so 5 tools with 100 - 90 = 10 cm left over. Cost: strip N800 + wire N300 + steel strip N400 + finish N200 = N1,700 for 5 modelling tools plus a wire and a loop tool.
precautions: Measure twice, cut once.
Finish the tools to prevent splinters and rust.
sourcesOfError: Saw cuts are about 2 mm wide (kerf), so each cut loses a little length.
commonMistakes: Leaving sharp metal edges.
Using softwood that splits.
examTips: Working drawings with dimensions and a list of materials earn marks.
State how to care for and maintain the tools: clean, dry and oil them.

checkQuestions.q: How many 15 cm tools can be cut from a 100 cm strip, ignoring the saw cut?
The cutting wire is used to
options: Cut clay and remove pots from the wheel
checkQuestions.explanation: The wire cuts clay and frees thrown pots.

checkQuestions.q: Metal tools are oiled after cleaning to prevent
checkQuestions.explanation: Oil keeps moisture off the steel.

practicals.title: Developing design ideas and scaled working drawings
practicals.aim: To develop ideas for a ceramic ware through sketches and produce a dimensioned working drawing that allows for shrinkage.
apparatus: Computer with a CAD or drawing program (optional)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Analyse the brief: the item, its function, size and theme.
Draw several thumbnail sketches of forms and decoration ideas from local sources.
Choose and refine one idea. Draw its front elevation, plan and a section showing wall thickness.
Add the fired dimensions, then work out and add the wet (making) dimensions.
Draw the decoration layout and a colour or glaze plan.
Cut a profile template from card for building or throwing.
practicals.expectedObservations: A dimensioned drawing gives a clear target during making, so the final ware is close to the size required.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A vase that must be 30 cm high when fired is drawn at 1:2, which is 15 cm on paper. With 11% total shrinkage the making height is 30 / 0.89 = 33.71 cm, and the drawing at 1:2 shows 16.85 cm for the wet form.
precautions: State the scale on every drawing.
Use fired sizes plus a shrinkage allowance.
Show sections clearly.
commonMistakes: Giving no scale or units.
Decoration that ignores the form.
examTips: Preparatory sketches and notes carry 20 marks. Show the development of ideas, not only the final drawing.
Include a time plan for the five days of execution.

checkQuestions.q: A 24 cm bowl drawn at 1:4 measures
With 10% shrinkage, a fired height of 27 cm needs a wet height of
A drawing that shows the cut-through wall thickness is a
checkQuestions.explanation: A section reveals the wall profile.

practicals.title: Costing and pricing a batch of flower vases
practicals.topic: Costing, pricing, packaging and marketing of ceramic objects
practicals.aim: To calculate the cost per item and the selling price of a batch of vases, allowing for firing losses.
materials: Price list for clay, glaze, fuel, packaging and transport
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: List the materials: clay, glaze and oxides.
Add the firing costs (fuel or electricity), labour, packaging and transport.
Find the total cost and divide it by the number of good (saleable) wares, not by the number made.
Add the markup and check the result against market prices from a market survey.
practicals.expectedObservations: Firing losses raise the cost of each saleable ware considerably.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Batch of 20 vases. Clay 25 kg x N600 = N15,000, glaze N8,000, fuel N12,000, labour N20,000, packaging N3,000, transport N4,000. Total N62,000. If all 20 survive, unit cost = N3,100 and the price at 30% markup is N4,030. If 2 crack in firing, unit cost = 62,000 / 18 = N3,444.44 and the price at 30% markup is N4,477.78, so sell at about N4,500.
precautions: Include every cost.
Allow for losses.
Compare with competitors' prices.
commonMistakes: Dividing by the number made rather than the number sold.
Forgetting labour.
examTips: Set out the costing in a table.
Mention packaging (protective padding, branded boxes) and marketing channels.

checkQuestions.q: A total cost of N45,000 for 15 good wares gives a unit cost of
A unit cost of N2,000 with a 50% markup gives a price of
Firing losses make the cost per saleable ware
checkQuestions.explanation: The same costs are shared by fewer wares.
